prompt: An unoptimised search for `\s+$` tries each space as a new starting point in a long run of spaces followed by x. Why can the total work be quadratic?

options.text: Only the final character is examined
options.explanation: Each attempt first scans spaces before failing at x.

options.text: Many starts each rescan a long overlapping suffix
options.explanation: Correct. Longer input creates more starts and more scanning per start.

options.text: The engine has exponentially many nested repetitions
options.explanation: This example needs no nested repetition; repeated starts are enough for polynomial growth.

options.text: A single pass stores every substring
options.explanation: The work comes from revisiting text, not necessarily storing substrings.

workedExample: At the first space, the attempt scans the whole run and fails at x. The next attempt repeats most of that work, then the next repeats slightly less. Summing the overlapping scans gives quadratic growth. A pattern can therefore be costly even without exponential ambiguity. Actual optimisations may change a particular implementation’s behaviour.

prompt: In an anchored, path-enumerating backtracker without memoization or pattern simplification, which patterns have exponentially many ambiguous paths on a run of n a characters followed by !? Select all that apply. (two to the power n means n copies of 2 multiplied together.)

options.explanation: Exponential: nested regex quantifiers give two raised to one less than n ways to split the a's.
Exponential: each a can be matched by either branch, giving two to the power n paths.
Not exponential. At a fixed start, a single regex repetition operator scans and may backtrack through linearly many match lengths.
Exponential. Since `\s?` can match nothing, this behaves like `(\w+)*` on a run of letters: nested regex quantifiers.
Not exponential. Each iteration of the group must end at a space, so a run of letters can be split only one way.

workedExample: The nested regex quantifiers in (a+)+ and (\w+\s?)* allow two raised to one less than n complete decompositions of a run of n a's. Duplicate alternatives in (a|a)* allow two to the power n branch sequences. The single-run a+ and mandatory-separator rewrite do not have that exponential ambiguity. These are conceptual path counts, not measured timings; optimizations may collapse duplicate alternatives.

prompt: A regex benchmark is fast on successful examples but slows sharply on longer almost-matches. What is the most useful next investigation?

options.text: Treat the successful timings as a worst-case guarantee
options.explanation: Success may be found early while failure explores many alternatives.

options.text: Infer an exact complexity class from three timings
options.explanation: A few timings cannot establish asymptotic behaviour or isolate fixed overhead.

options.text: Assume every regex engine uses the same algorithm
options.explanation: Libraries and APIs use different strategies and optimisations.

options.text: Inspect ambiguous paths and restart behaviour, then test bounded failing inputs
options.explanation: Correct. Explain the repeated work and check it under the actual engine and API.

workedExample: Construct controlled almost-matches that force the late failure. Check whether the engine revisits equivalent state/position pairs or restarts searches across overlapping suffixes. Use bounded tests and resource limits. Measurements help test the explanation, but documented guarantees and the mechanism are needed before generalising.

prompt: In full matching by a path-enumerating backtracker, `(a|aa)*` can consume an a-run in one- or two-character pieces. A final ! makes every complete decomposition fail. What explains the growth?

options.text: There is exactly one path because both alternatives use a
options.explanation: The same input can be divided into different piece lengths.

options.text: Each choice leaves a shorter run with the same branching problem
options.explanation: Correct. One-character and two-character first pieces lead to overlapping subproblems, giving Fibonacci growth.

options.text: Removing nested quantifiers guarantees linear time
options.explanation: Overlapping alternatives under a repetition can still create exponential ambiguity.

options.text: The letters must be permuted into different orders
options.explanation: Their order never changes; only the boundaries between repetitions differ.

workedExample: For four a characters, possible groupings include four single pieces, two double pieces, or a double piece and two singles in several orders. A longer run can begin with either a single or double piece; each remainder branches again. Without merging or memoisation this produces exponentially many decompositions, even though the growth factor is smaller than doubling.
